subject: Chemistry
title: Classification of Elements and Periodicity
summary: Mendeleev arranged elements by atomic mass and left gaps for undiscovered ones. Moseley showed atomic number is more fundamental, giving the modern periodic law: properties are periodic functions of atomic number.
The long form table has 18 groups and 7 periods, divided into s-, p-, d- and f-blocks by the subshell receiving the last electron.
Periodic trends come from effective nuclear charge and shielding: across a period atoms shrink and hold electrons more tightly; down a group they grow and hold electrons less tightly.
Key trends: atomic/ionic radius, ionisation enthalpy, electron gain enthalpy, electronegativity and valence. Exceptions (N vs O, Be vs B, F vs Cl) are exam favourites.

formulas.name: Modern periodic law
formulas.formula: properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers

formulas.name: Position from configuration
formulas.formula: period = highest n;  s-block group = valence e⁻;  p-block group = 10 + valence e⁻ (ns + np);  d-block group = ns + (n − 1)d electrons
formulas.when: Finding period, group and block from Z.

formulas.name: Effective nuclear charge
formulas.when: Explaining all size and energy trends.

formulas.name: Atomic radius trend
formulas.formula: decreases across a period, increases down a group;  noble gases quoted as van der Waals radii
formulas.mistake: Don't compare a noble gas's van der Waals radius with covalent radii of other elements.

formulas.name: Ionic radius
formulas.formula: cation < parent atom < anion;  isoelectronic species: higher Z → smaller
formulas.when: N³⁻ > O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺ > Al³⁺.

formulas.name: Ionisation enthalpy
formulas.formula: IE₁ < IE₂ < IE₃ …;  increases across a period, decreases down a group
formulas.note: Exceptions: B < Be and O < N (stable 2s² and half-filled 2p³). Period 3 too: Mg > Al (stable 3s²; Al loses an easy 3p¹ electron) and P > S (half-filled 3p³), so Na < Al < Mg < Si < S < P.

formulas.name: Electron gain enthalpy
formulas.formula: more negative across a period, less negative down a group;  Cl has the most negative value
formulas.when: Energy change on adding an electron.
formulas.note: F is less negative than Cl — its small 2p shell repels the incoming electron.

formulas.name: Electronegativity (Pauling)
formulas.formula: increases across, decreases down;  F 4.0 > O 3.5 > N 3.0 = Cl 3.0 (N and Cl are the SAME on the Pauling scale)

formulas.name: Metallic and non-metallic character
formulas.formula: metallic character decreases across, increases down
formulas.when: Nature of oxides: basic → amphoteric → acidic across a period.

formulas.name: Valence
formulas.formula: s/p-block: valence = group electrons or 8 − group electrons
formulas.when: Writing formulas of compounds (e.g. Al₂O₃) and predicting common oxidation states.

examples.title: Position of Z = 33
examples.problem: Element with Z = 33: period and block?

examples.title: Shielding estimate
examples.problem: Using simple shielding (inner shell 1s² = 1.0 each, 2s²2p⁶ = 0.85 each), estimate Z_eff for the 3s electron of Na.
examples.solution: Z_eff = 11 − (2 × 1.0 + 8 × 0.85) = 2.2 — so the outer electron is held weakly and Na loses it easily.

examples.title: Ordering ionic radii
examples.problem: Arrange Na⁺, F⁻, Mg²⁺, O²⁻ by size.
examples.solution: All have 10 electrons; more protons pull harder: O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺.

examples.title: Ionisation enthalpy order
examples.problem: Arrange B, C, N, O by first ionisation enthalpy.
examples.solution: B < C < O < N. N (2p³, half-filled) is extra stable; O loses a paired 2p electron more easily.

examples.title: Most negative electron gain enthalpy
examples.problem: Which has the most negative electron gain enthalpy: F, Cl, Br, O?
examples.solution: Cl. F is smaller, so electron–electron repulsion in its compact 2p shell makes its value less negative than Cl's.

topics.title: History of classification
topics.explain: Döbereiner's triads (Li, Na, K), Newlands' law of octaves, Lothar Meyer's volume curves, and Mendeleev's periodic table (1869), which predicted eka-aluminium (Ga) and eka-silicon (Ge). Moseley (1913) showed that atomic number orders elements correctly.

topics.title: Blocks of the table
topics.explain: s-block (groups 1, 2): reactive metals, low IE. p-block (13–18): metals, metalloids and non-metals, including halogens and noble gases. d-block (3–12): transition metals, variable valency, coloured ions. f-block: lanthanoids and actinoids at the bottom.

topics.title: Nomenclature of new elements
topics.explain: Elements with Z > 100 get temporary IUPAC names from digit roots: 0 nil, 1 un, 2 bi, 3 tri, 4 quad, 5 pent, 6 hex, 7 sept, 8 oct, 9 enn + 'ium'. Z = 120 is unbinilium (Ubn).

topics.title: Why trends happen
topics.explain: Across a period electrons enter the same shell while nuclear charge rises, so Z_eff increases: smaller radius, higher IE, more negative electron gain enthalpy, higher electronegativity. Down a group a new shell is added and shielding grows, so the trends reverse.

topics.title: Anomalous behaviour of the first element
topics.explain: The first element of each group (Li, Be, B, C, N, O, F) differs from the rest: small size, high electronegativity, no d orbitals (maximum covalency 4). Diagonal relationship: Li–Mg, Be–Al, B–Si show similar properties.

topics.title: Chemical reactivity and oxides
topics.explain: Reactivity is highest at the two ends of a period (alkali metals, halogens). Oxides change from strongly basic (Na₂O) through amphoteric (Al₂O₃) to strongly acidic (Cl₂O₇) across period 3.

ratta: Modern law: periodic in atomic number (Moseley).
Period = highest n;  p-block group = 10 + ns + np electrons.
Radius ↓ across, ↑ down;  isoelectronic: more Z → smaller.
Most negative electron gain enthalpy: Cl (not F).
Oxides across period 3: basic → amphoteric → acidic.
IE period 3: Na 496 < Al 577 < Mg 737 < Si 786 kJ/mol (Mg > Al, P > S).
Ga melts at only 303 K (melts in the hand) — very low like Cs (~302 K), not high.
